prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change, task content and trade exposure reshape labour demand, wage inequality and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: I ranked B032 first in my opening because Kiyotaki-Moore is a foundational mechanism, and I still think so. After reading the openings, I move my preferred prize to B006 on common criteria. It joins a conceptual framework (tasks, the skill premium, the race between education and technology) to credible quasi-experimental evidence on import competition and local labour markets. The papers span roughly 1992 to 2016, so the China-shock results have been replicated, extended across countries and contested for a decade, and the core findings have survived that scrutiny. It also bears on distribution, trade adjustment and technological change, which are among the central questions of the period. Its influence reaches labour, trade, macro and public policy. B032 has a clean and mature mechanism, but it is a single-paper foundation with indirect empirical support. Only one other member ranks it, so I do not see a case that would carry it against B006 on scientific breadth and confirmation.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the strongest reservation. Dorn is a central co-author of the China-shock papers and is left out by the three-name cap. The task framework rests partly on contributors outside the credited list. Katz's best-known skill-premium work overlaps with Goldin's 2023 recognition, and the task-model theory overlaps with Acemoglu's 2024 recognition. The persistence and magnitude of the trade-shock effects remain debated. There is a real risk that this is two discoveries (technology and trade) joined under one citation. A committee that wants a cleaner, narrower prize could reasonably prefer B007, whose credit is better documented.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B006 second and B007 first. He accepts the merit of B006 but notes that the task-model lineage has important contributors outside the credited set, which complicates attribution.
responses.response: I agree that the lineage point is real, and I take it as a constraint on the citation, not as a reason to demote the work. Our citation should name the empirical and conceptual achievement (tasks, skill demand, trade exposure) and avoid claiming ownership of the whole task theory. I differ on B007. Its credit is cleaner than B006's, but I do not think that offsets B006's wider confirmation and policy reach, and the 2024 institutions prize makes the timing for B007 less comfortable. I keep B007 as my first alternative for that reason.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B006 first. He sees the task framework and the China-shock evidence as changing how economists and policymakers think about labour demand. He flags that Dorn, Levy and Murnane are not in the three-name set and that Hanson and Katz are uneven picks.
responses.response: I agree on influence and replication. On attribution I would qualify slightly. The three-person set is defensible if the citation is built around the common achievement and not around specific papers. Dorn's claim is strong, and I would accept a substitution of Dorn for Katz if the committee decides the trade-shock evidence is the core. Katz is the weaker fit for that strand, since his contribution is the skill-premium and education-technology line. I include him because that line gives the long-run framework that makes the trade evidence interpretable, but this is a judgement the committee should test, not a settled point.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B032 sixth and notes that Kiyotaki-Moore are the clear originators of the collateral-constraint mechanism. He also notes that the Gertler-Gilchrist line has been partly recognised by the 2022 prize and that the original model has limited direct empirical testing.
responses.response: This is a fair challenge to my own opening ranking. The overlap with 2022 is not decisive, since collateral-constrained amplification is distinct from the bank-run and bank-intermediation work, but the thin direct empirical testing is a real weakness next to B006's replication record. Having thought about it, I treat B032 as a strong but narrower contribution and keep it as an alternative, not the preferred prize.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B006 first but warns that the 2023 and 2024 prizes in labour and technology topics may reduce the marginal case. He adds that the trade-shock persistence debate is unresolved.
responses.response: The overlap concern is the best argument against my preferred option, and I take it seriously. My answer is that the 2023 and 2024 prizes covered the long-run gender gap and institutions and growth, and neither covered the trade-exposure evidence or the empirical task approach. I would still require the citation to stay away from ground those prizes already covered. The persistence debate does not undermine the discovery, because a contested magnitude is not the same as an unconfirmed finding.

uncertainties: Whether the third laureate should be Katz or Dorn, and whether the committee views the technology and trade strands as one coherent discovery or two.
How much the 2023 (Goldin) and 2024 (Acemoglu) prizes reduce the marginal case for B006, which depends on how narrowly the citation can be framed.
The long-run persistence and magnitude of China-shock effects, and the generalisability of the findings beyond the US episode.
Whether B007's cleaner attribution should outweigh B006's broader confirmation and policy reach, given the 2024 institutions prize.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the B006 candidates is apparent from the supplied profile. I disclose ties to colleagues that bear on how I read their arguments: I co-authored with Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg, I am an IIES colleague of Per Krusell and Boppart, and Krusell is a frequent co-author. None of them is a credited name on B006. B032, B007 and B009 are not tied to my own work in the supplied profile. My opening disclosed my own mobility research, but I do not prefer B050.
